1:
Henry opens by warning that the chapter resists division. Its particulars are dispersed and interwoven, the same things left and returned to so often that the exposition must gather them under heads rather than follow the order of the verses. Gill makes the same point: this is no new prophecy but the enlargement of the last, the Babylonians dwelt on at such length because they were the final and most notorious enemies of the Jews, and because as they were against the Lord's people the Lord was against them. Clarke sets out the whole argument in advance, the sudden and final ruin of a people who had compelled the nations to receive their idolatrous rites, and marks one figure as awfully sublime, the sea coming up upon the city and covering her with the multitude of its waves. Calvin answers the obvious objection before it is made. The prophet seems to use more words than necessary; but the event was hardly credible, and a thing no one would admit had to be illustrated with many figures, inculcated by repetition, and confirmed by many reasons.

The destroying wind divides them. Ellicott renders it strictly as the wind of a destroyer and notes that the phrase is used elsewhere for stirring up the spirit of a man, which may be its sense here; but the fanners of the next verse pull toward the plain meaning of wind, and he suggests it was used first so and acquired a figurative sense after. Calvin thinks the similitude very appropriate, since it reminds men how easily God could destroy the whole world by a single blast, and he hears in it a contrast with the instruments of war: a man who means to overcome an enemy gathers forces and procures auxiliaries on every side and dares attempt nothing without every preparation, whereas God has only to raise a wind. God is made the speaker, he adds, so that the word may carry more force.

The cipher in the second half of the verse is Ellicott's find and he presses it hard. The Hebrew behind the English clause means literally in the heart of my adversaries, and in the judgment of most commentators the two words are another instance of the letter-cipher already met with in this book, by which the phrase resolves into the name of the Chaldeans. The significance of the plain words gives point to the choice of the cipher rather than replacing it, and the device parallels the symbolic names used of the same enemy earlier. He records that the Greek and Syriac versions both translate against the Chaldeans, and that these cipher-words had probably become familiar in the correspondence between the exiles and their countrymen left at home, so that both parties would understand them. Calvin, working the same clause, finds an obscurity in the construction and supplies the country of the Chaldeans as what the grammar wants.

On the fanners the readings turn on a vowel. Ellicott observes that the word as it stands means strangers, and that a change of pointing would give winnowers, a form found nowhere else; he prefers strangers, taking the prophet to have set it beside the verb for fanning, which shares its consonants, for the sake of the assonance. Gill gives both and names the agents, the Medes and Persians, a strong wind on the threshing mountains carrying the chaff away. Clarke describes the floor itself, the corn trodden out by cattle or crushed by a heavy iron-armed wheel and then thrown up with a shovel against the wind. Calvin doubts the sense of aliens as harsh and keeps the allusion to the wind already mentioned. Keil and Delitzsch turn to the doubled verb of the following verse, where the Masoretic note would expunge a repetition, and conclude that the meaning is not thereby changed.
3:
The summons to the archers is read as a rhetorical device before a command. Ellicott points out that the Hebrew for archer is literally bender, so the iteration of the verb gains its full force, and that the coat of mail names the heavy-armed troops, the two classes together standing for the whole garrison of the city. Gill leaves the speaker open: either the Lord addresses the bowmen of the Medes and Persians, bidding them level their arrows against those who had shot at others, or the invaders stir one another up to fight manfully. Calvin finds interpreters divided over whether one clause describes light armour and the other heavy, and over whether a particle here is negative; he judges the second copulative redundant and a relative understood before the first verb. His literal rendering keeps the play the English loses: at him who bends let the bender bend his bow, and at him who glories in his coat of mail, and spare ye not.

The slain fall in two places and the pairing is the point. Gill has them cut down by the sword and by the arrows and darts of the invaders alike. Calvin takes the doubling to mean they would be killed not only in the open fields but in the middle of the city, and adds that however powerful the armies Babylon prepared it would be in vain, since a city so populous could not be overthrown without the calamity reaching through the whole country. Keil and Delitzsch supply the connective the verses leave implicit: it is for the righteousness of Israel that Babylon is irretrievably destroyed.

The clause about Israel not being forsaken produces the tile's richest disagreement, and it turns on a single participle. Ellicott corrects the rendering to widowed, the participle coming from the word that ordinarily carries that idea, and reads the whole as a denial of what men supposed: Judah and Israel were not abandoned by their husband, who was still their protector. He hears at once the image of apparent widowhood found in other prophets and the thought that the husband is ready to forgive, and insists the assurance rests on no plea in extenuation of the guilt the following words admit without reserve; he would read her or their for his, to keep the metaphor intact. Calvin reaches the same figure and presses it further. The exile looked like a repudiation, and while their enemies prevailed God seemed to have forsaken them; they were for a time like widows, but the divorce was temporary, the church having been united to God from the beginning as by a marriage-bond. Clarke takes the verse differently, of prophets still sent among them and mercy remembered in the midst of deserved punishment, and proposes that the word rendered sin means punishment, a sense it often carries. Wesley compresses the whole to two words: not utterly forsaken.

On the flight from the city the question is who is addressed. Gill reports two answers, that it is spoken to foreigners there on business or to the captive Jews, and notes its application to the mystical city. Ellicott says the call reproduces an earlier one with a fresh motive: the city was doomed, and it was ill done for those innocent of her sins to share her ruin. Keil and Delitzsch fix the disputed preposition against two other scholars: not in her guilt nor through her guilt but at the price of it, since Israel must flee to save his life and not atone for the guilt of Babylon. Calvin explains why the exhortation was needed at all, since there was then no safer place on earth, and remarks that were anyone now to predict the fall of a great city it would hardly be believed. Wesley glosses the two nouns, soul as life and iniquity as the punishment of it.
7:
The golden cup is glossed by everyone. Gill offers three accounts of the gold: the liquor in it, yellow or pure as gold, the general reading of the Jewish commentators; the material, standing for the riches of an empire elsewhere called a head of gold; or the contents, since by permission of God the city had drawn the nations into idolatry and other sins, which were as poison in a golden cup. Keil and Delitzsch take the gold to mark the splendour of the reigning dynasty, and note the figure is borrowed from an earlier chapter of this book where it is applied differently. Ellicott agrees the gold points to outward splendour but insists the wine was poisoned, intoxicating men with wild ambitions and dark idolatries, and traces the image into the apocalypse, where the cup is in the harlot's hand. Clarke reads the cup as the plenitude of punishment inflicted on transgressors, intoxicating and making men mad.

Calvin answers an objection with it. Kingdoms neither rise nor stand except by God's will, so a hearer might ask how the city the prophet calls accursed had flourished so long, since no monarchy is elevated so high by chance. God was not inconsistent with himself when he used the Babylonians as his scourge and now chastises them in their turn.

The suddenness of the fall is agreed. Gill has the cup dashed in pieces like a potter's vessel, the ruin brought about in a very short time considering the strength of the place, unexpected by all around, and once come, irreparable. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the prophet drops the figure at exactly this point, since a golden cup does not break when it falls. Calvin makes the suddenness the doctrine: God can accomplish in one moment what he has decreed, needing no warlike forces, since without preparation he can subvert every power in the world. Clarke puts the announcement in the mouth of spectators.

The call to take balm is where they part. Ellicott calls the words significant and refuses to let them be a shout of triumph. The captive people are not invited merely to exult over their oppressor's fall; they are to take balm, in an image used twice before in this book, and try to heal her, still seeking the peace of the city. Calvin hears irony instead, and reports a dispute over the word rendered balm. Gill leaves the speakers open: either the allies who did all they could to defend her, or the prophets and good people among the exiles who laboured to convince the inhabitants of their idolatries and were answered with nothing. He applies the failure to later reformers. Clarke has it that had it been in their power they would have saved her, but they could not turn away the judgment of God. Calvin reads the speakers as physicians by metaphor, the subject nations and hired soldiers called in as a great prince sends everywhere for the most skilful when he is taken ill, pleading afterwards that the fault was not theirs. Wesley takes the same view, that the prophet personates the mercenary soldiers. Ellicott alone makes it the exiles answering the prophet, having done what they could in vain.

On the righteousness brought forth, Gill insists it is not the righteousness of their persons but of their cause, since they had committed much iniquity and were righteous only by comparison. Ellicott notes the noun is plural, the many righteous acts, and reads the exile as a time of reformation, the day of vengeance being also a day of acquittal. Clarke makes it the answer of the Jews, that God has vindicated their cause. Calvin finds a proof of paternal favour toward the church and an exhortation to gratitude, Wesley the owning of the ruin as the mighty work of God avenging his people.
11:
Making bright the arrows is a lexical question and everyone takes a turn at it. Gill has them covered with rust, to be scoured and oiled so they may pierce deeper; the word is equally rendered sharpen, as in the Targum, and also carries the sense of choosing, though a lexicographer he cites notes that either way the end is the same. Ellicott prefers sharpen outright, the polishing being the means to it. On the next clause he is more insistent: the Hebrew is literally fill the shields, meaning arm yourselves with them, since the large Persian shields covered the whole body. The Greek and Latin render quivers, which he calls a conjecture meant to connect the clauses. Calvin canvasses the same options and settles on shields.

Who is addressed is disputed twice over. Calvin allows the words to be spoken to the Medes or to the Babylonians: on the second a taunt, that they spend their labour to no purpose preparing armies, since God is stronger and the Medes campaign under his authority; on the first a summons to arm. Clarke reads it as the prophet's address to Babylon and supplies the history, naming the Median king called elsewhere in scripture by another name, and the Persian prince sent with thirty thousand men to assist his uncle.

The standard on the walls divides them the same way. Gill rejects the flag of victory, since the city has not yet fallen in what follows, and makes it an ironical order to the Babylonians to gather the inhabitants to their bulwarks. Wesley agrees, rousing them out of their security, and adds from the historians that the walls stood fifty cubits high and two hundred broad. Clarke takes it the other way, a call to the enemy to invest the city. Ellicott notes that the received version follows the old translations in reading an ironical summons to a fruitless defence, but the preposition may mean against, which suits the context better; then the standards signal an attack at a chosen point, the watchmen are scouts against a sally, and the ambush is either any sudden attack or a feigned flight. Keil and Delitzsch state the argument: neither the strong position on the river nor the treasures that paid for the fortifications can avert what God has decreed.

The many waters are explained physically and then allegorized. Calvin describes the river not merely flowing past the city but surrounding it, divided above into many streams so that it made as it were many islands; the channels were navigable and the land more fertile for their irrigation, serving wealth as well as defence. Wesley says the same briefly. Gill turns the situation to the mystical city said to sit on many waters, interpreted of peoples and nations; Clarke allows both senses. Ellicott brings an inscription of the king himself, boasting that he made water flow all around in an immense dyke of earth and carried an aqueduct across great waters like the depths of the sea.

The oath is read for its condescension. Gill takes swearing by himself as swearing by his soul, than which he could swear by no greater, the design being to remove hesitation. Calvin presses further: swearing by one's own soul is a man's way of pledging his life, so that a perjurer forfeits it, which suits men and not God at all; what does not properly belong to God is transferred to him, and the more familiar the speech the more it ought to touch men. Ellicott calls it the most solemn form of affirmation, corrects caterpillars to locusts as the fullest type of the destroyer's swarms, and identifies the shout as the cry of those treading the winepress. Clarke makes the filling concrete: by those very boasted waters the city shall be filled with men rising unexpectedly from the channel of the river.
15:
These five verses are a quotation, and Clarke says so outright: they are transcribed from an earlier chapter of this book. Calvin knows it and makes the repetition the interesting thing. The words were used before to a different end, when the prophet bade the exiles stand firm though religion was oppressed and the Chaldeans derided it, teaching them a sentence in a foreign tongue to say on arrival, that cursed are all the gods who made not the heaven and the earth. Here the purpose has changed. The faithful were not to judge the empire by the splendour that dazzled every eye, but to raise their thoughts above the world and behold an incomprehensible power, since what the flesh held impossible could easily be done. He notes too that the divine name is withheld in the first clause, and finds the omission the more emphatic for it. Keil and Delitzsch put the logic of the quotation in one sentence: the omnipotence of the Creator of the world will destroy the idols of Babylon and break the kingdom that rules it.

Clarke takes the three clauses of the first verse as three attributes, each with its evidence. Omnipotence is manifested in the works of creation; omniscience in the government of the inhabited globe, in the skill apparent in the providence that supplies every living thing; and deep thought in the magnitudes, distances and revolutions of the heavenly bodies. On the thunder and rain he turns natural philosopher of his own century, deriving the water from an electric spark decomposing the air, the clouds from evaporation that rarefies water until it is lighter than air, and the winds from currents formed by lightning and heat.

Calvin comes at the same phenomena from the opposite end. Philosophers do assign causes, but one ought to come to the original cause, since the world is so arranged that though there are subordinate causes the primary one always appears eminently. Winds arise from the earth because exhalations proceed from it; but the exhalations are not created by themselves, so God is their sole author.

On the idols comes the sharpest passage. Clarke gives the double sense of the reproach: a man is brutish for want of real knowledge, and brutish again when he acknowledges that an idol is anything in the world. Calvin sets aside the usual reading, which takes the verse for a general account of how men glide into error by seeking to be wise on their own terms. The context, he insists, means something narrower: the craftsmen who cast or forge idols are delirious in thinking their art can make gods. A log lies on the ground trodden underfoot without honour; the artificer adds a form, and it begins to be worshipped. The same holds of stone and gold, for no divinity is ascribed to the metal until it puts on a shape. He notes an impropriety in the pairing of the graven with the founder and explains it as a part standing for the whole. The proof offered is that there is no breath in them, which he calls sufficient, since God is the fountain of life. He turns the argument against those who defend images as books for the unlearned, an evasion suggested long ago and, he says, very foolishly.

The closing contrast is what Calvin most wants. To say idols are impostures would be something, but the teaching would be cold had the glory of the one true God not been proclaimed on the other side. The vanity already named cannot be understood until the true God is known; the ancient philosophers ridiculed the grosser errors of the common people but had nothing fixed to rest on, like the one who, asked what God was, requested time and after several delays confessed that the more he inquired the more his thoughts were absorbed.
20:
Who is the hammer is the whole question here, and it is not settled. Gill inclines to the conqueror raised up to subdue nations, but thinks it likelier to be Babylon and her king, called the hammer of the whole earth in the previous chapter; though God had used the city to destroy others, she would not herself be secure. He allows a third possibility, that the kingdom of Christ is meant, which in the latter day breaks all the kingdoms of the earth. Clarke believes the reigning king of Babylon is meant, records that others apply it to the Persian, and insists all the verbs are past: with thee have I broken in pieces. Ellicott arrives at the opposite conclusion. He corrects the rendering to mace, since the axe does not appear on Assyrian monuments as a weapon of war until comparatively late, and, weighing Babylon, the conqueror and Israel, judges the conqueror the more probable, so that the hammer of the whole earth is broken by a mightier weapon. Against Clarke he holds the tenses should be present, the force of the verb multiplied by its emphatic iteration.

Calvin sets out both readings and the grammar behind them. Many take the verbs as future and understand the Persian by the hammer, but render the attached pronoun in a way the accents and versions do not support; the more consistent view, given what follows, is that Babylon was the hammer God had employed, and that he would hereafter employ a hammer within Babylon itself. His own rendering keeps the preposition where the Hebrew puts it: a scatterer art thou to me, a weapon of war, but I will scatter in thee nations and destroy in thee kingdoms. The verb means both to break in pieces and to scatter.

Behind the philology he has a doctrine ready. The objection expected is that a monarchy fortified by so many defences and holding its neighbours in subjection was impregnable. The answer is drawn from the contrary: the Chaldeans had not raised themselves but had been raised and employed, so that Babylon is a formed vessel and God the potter, as in the sign the prophet was sent to watch. It belongs to him who raised the city so high to pull it down when he pleases.

The catalogue of what is broken is read as exhaustive. Gill glosses the pairs as they come: the horse and rider meaning the cavalry, in which an army's chief strength lies; man and woman, with no respect to sex or to posterity; the shepherd and his flock, which one Jewish commentator refers to the tent-dwelling Arabians, though Gill takes it generally of shepherds killed wherever the armies came, sparing none however innocent. Ellicott observes that the exhausting of all sorts and conditions of men culminates in the ruling caste, the Hebrew for captain being connected with an Arabic word familiar in a later form. Wesley treats the three verses as one sentence with one sense, that God had used and was still using the Babylonians to destroy many nations.

The turn at the end hangs on one conjunction, and Clarke will not let it pass: the particle should be translated but, of which it has here the full force. Gill renders it the same way and extends the recompense from the city to the whole land. Calvin faces the difficulty this creates. If their service depended on God's command they would seem to deserve praise, and elsewhere a prophet has God giving Egypt to the same king as wages for his work. Both declarations agree, he holds: the reward had regard to a people not yet humbled, who thought they had been subdued by chance, whereas this promise is given peculiarly to the church, so the faithful might know the covenant had never failed, and in the midst of death have some hope.
25:
Calling a city on a plain a mountain needs explaining. Calvin states the difficulty: the place lay in a flat country with no hills near it. The usual answer is the height of the walls, which he thinks probable, and he supplies figures from the historians, walls of some two hundred feet and towers higher still. Gill gives the same reasons, adds the hanging gardens, and offers a second: monarchies are usually compared to mountains. Wesley combines both, high in greatness and high in its walls, so that at a distance it looked like a rocky mountain. Ellicott finds what none of the others notice. The phrase is the same applied elsewhere to the Mount of Olives and rendered there the Mount of Corruption; that name was given in the reign of the king under whom this prophet began, and marked a hill that had been the centre of a foreign worship destroying the faith of Israel. Here it carries the thought that Babylon's false worship was the root of her evils.

Clarke reads the mountain as a volcano. The government vomits streams of lava over the towns and fields near it; when the matter in its bowels is exhausted it will stand an extinguished crater, and what it has cast out will not be of substance enough for a foundation stone or a corner stone. Gill takes the clause literally, the city so consumed that no stone would be left fit for any new building, and notes the Targum understands it figuratively. Ellicott is drier: the language would fit any city destroyed by fire, without noting that this one was built of bricks. Calvin answers the objection: the prophet speaks in the common manner to show the ruin would be for ever. Cities wholly destroyed are often built again, but this one was given over to perpetual desolation.

The summons to the nations brings in the geography. Gill sets the standard not in Chaldea but in the countries belonging to the invading power, to enlist soldiers. Clarke identifies the three kingdoms as the Greater and Lesser Armenia and a part of Phrygia near the Hellespont. Ellicott is more cautious. The first name was unknown to Greek and Roman geographers, is elsewhere translated Armenia, and is Sanskrit for the holy land. The second has not been identified and occurs nowhere else, though something like it appears in the Assyrian inscriptions. The word for prepare, he adds, carries the idea of consecration. Calvin makes the imperative the point: the unbelieving deride whatever they hear, the voice of God being to them a sound in the air, so the prophet shows he was endued with power by commanding the nations to war. Wesley glosses the locust comparison as touching the numbers of the horses or the terror they caused.

On the kings of the Medes the versions divide, and Calvin sides with the singular, which the phrase his dominion at the end requires; he explains the plural anyway, one kingdom holding many provinces under satraps. Gill names two rulers at their head. Ellicott reaches the same result from the pronoun: it shows kings, captains and rulers all under one sovereign leader. Keil and Delitzsch describe what the prophet sees: the earth quaking at the advance of the host, the mighty men ceasing to resist and withdrawing dispirited while the enemy fires the houses and breaks the bars, all viewed in spirit as already present. Ellicott makes the same point grammatically: the verbs stand in the past because the prophet sees the event passing before him. Gill and Clarke keep to the plain sense, the inhabitants in pain as a woman in travail and the ground shaking under the armies. Calvin hears a deliberate contrast: though the whole earth were moved, the purpose of God stands confirmed, the verb properly meaning to rise but here necessarily to establish.
30:
The capture is narrated rather than expounded, and the expositors reach for the secular historians. Calvin says the prophet shows the manner of it as by the finger, exactly as the heathen authors describe it: the city was taken by craft rather than open force, the besieger having been laughed to scorn after a long siege while the Babylonians securely feasted; two eunuchs of the king went over to him, one whose son the tyrant had killed and one he had castrated by way of disgrace, and from them the besieger learned how the place could be taken. The fords were dried when no such thing was suspected, and in the night the king heard that the city was his no longer. Gill has the defenders give battle at the enemy's first coming, retire into the city overthrown, and never dare fight again. Clarke says they were panic-struck to find the invaders inside their walls and saw resistance was useless. Ellicott takes the burning to be the invaders' work, houses set alight and the river-gates broken open while the people fled to their citadel. Keil and Delitzsch treat the messages as a continuation of what is brought to the king.

On the runners the point everyone seizes is the size of the place. Clarke reports from an ancient historian that the extreme parts were taken before those at the centre knew anything of the invasion. Ellicott says the words answer exactly to that account, and adds that the feast recorded in another book must have ended in a like result; no words, he thinks, could paint the panic of a surprised city more vividly. Calvin explains why they were unprepared to believe it: the walls were too high for the engines of that age, and being fifty feet thick, wide enough for four horses abreast, no battering-ram could throw them down, while the drying of the fords seemed simply incredible. Gill has the posts meeting as they come from different quarters, one returning from his errand as the next sets out. Wesley states the stratagem flatly: the enemy entered at one end by the channel of the river he had drained.

The stopped passages and the burnt reeds produce the tile's real division. Gill takes the passages for the gates leading from the river to the city, left open that night and now held by soldiers, though a Jewish commentator understands the riverside towers instead. Ellicott judges them the ferries by which one part of the city communicated with the other, at the ends of the streets running at right angles to the river; he notes there was besides one bridge in the middle and a tunnel beneath. Both he and Keil and Delitzsch reject the rendering fords, which the word bears elsewhere, since the river was not fordable there. Wesley adds the guards set to prevent escape. On the reeds Clarke confesses himself beaten: he cannot tell what it means unless it refers to something done after the capture, the firing of the marsh reeds to clear the ground, and he reports a scholar who takes it of firing the houses, observing that no historian mentions it. Ellicott notes the word is elsewhere translated pool and thinks it refers to a great artificial pool. Wesley makes the reeds a defence in themselves, vast tall growth along the bank which with the mud served as another wall until the invaders burned it and the way lay open. Calvin will have none of it. The word is metaphor and the literal rendering misplaced; the prophet says hyperbolically that the fords were dried as though one had set fire to wood, which does not suit water at all, and so expresses the miracle more fully. He takes the verse as proving the prophet a herald of God, setting out the capture as though he had watched it.
33:
The threshing-floor is glossed uniformly and then turned. Clarke says the wheel has gone over her and she is trodden underfoot. Ellicott corrects the rendering, the floor being in the time when it is trodden, that is, when it is prepared for the work, and resolves the ambiguity of her harvest: the heaped treasures are the crop her conquerors reap, the city itself the floor on which men trample the plunder. Wesley reverses the roles: the city had been the instrument and the floor on which God threshed other nations, and now becomes the floor where the Chaldeans are threshed in turn. Gill takes his cue from the two divine titles, omnipotence and the covenant name pledging that Israel's cause is pleaded. Keil and Delitzsch give the ground of judgment in a line: it comes on Babylon for its offences against Israel.

Calvin rejects the sense the interpreters have imagined. A threshing-floor serves only at harvest and is shut up the rest of the year; the city had long been such a closed floor, without treading, that is, without noise or shouting, and God declares it will now be used. In Judea, he notes, the corn was trodden by oxen rather than beaten with flails as in most parts of France. The similitude confirms what has been said about the time of visitation, since it seemed strange to promise deliverance while the monarchy was still enlarging. He appeals to another prophet, where husbandmen are the argument: they do not sow wheat and barley at once, nor always plough or reap, but wait for the seasonable times; and if a farmer has such foresight, why should God not have his own times distributed?

The complaint of the plundered is read as deliberate. Keil and Delitzsch identify the speakers as the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem, in whose name the crimes are enumerated. Ellicott notes that one form of the text has the pronouns plural, devoured us and crushed us, takes the swallowing creature for a crocodile or sea-monster, and glosses the delicates as the corn and wine and oil on which the invading armies grew rich. Clarke hears a promise inside it, that the swallower shall vomit all up and the spoil be regained. Gill reads the clauses as spoiled substance, cities plundered and the people carried away.

Calvin works the verbs one by one. On the pronouns he weighs the manuscripts as nearly equal and prefers the singular. To devour would have been enough, but the prophet wanted something more atrocious, adding a verb whose common sense is to disturb violently but which is used elsewhere of crushing. The king had not eaten like a man but like a wild beast that breaks the very bones.

The plea for retribution closes the passage and Calvin makes it a lesson. Having shown that the people's calamities were not unknown to God, the prophet exhorts the faithful to deposit their complaints in his bosom, so that in extreme evils we may learn to unburden our anxieties there, as the psalm bids us roll our cares upon him. Sorrow overwhelms us, he says, because we do not follow what the Spirit prescribes, but murmur and clamour, or at least champ the bridle. The weight of the plea lies in the blood, since the Chaldeans thought they had been cruel with impunity, yet innocent blood cried out against them. Ellicott keeps the reptile imagery running, Zion asking that the law of retribution be applied to what devoured her flesh and blood. Clarke marks the structure: the plundered city begins to speak at the swallowing and ends with this verse, the divine answer beginning in the next; and though the Chaldeans were God's instrument, being themselves exceedingly wicked they shall suffer for the blood they shed. Gill puts the plea simply, that the injuries to persons and families be avenged.
36:
The drying of the sea is the one real crux. Clarke disposes of it in five words: exhaust all her treasures. Ellicott lays out the range: some refer the sea to the confluent nations and the city's wealth to the springs that fed her greatness; others take it of the river, or of the plain cut by canals in which the city stood, so often flooded it became an actual sea. The Hebrew for springs is singular and means her reservoir; the two senses probably run together. Wesley points to what the conqueror did to the river. Calvin passes the philology by for the doctrine: we must present our complaints to God if we wish him to undertake our cause, for when we are silent he rests in his turn, but if we cry he hears. He insists on the order, the pleading first and the vengeance after. Gill marks the connection, that the answer comes to the prayers of Zion.

On the heaps they agree. Gill has the houses demolished, the stones lying one upon another as rubbish. Ellicott finds it significant, as emphasising retribution, that the terms are those used of Jerusalem earlier in this book, and remarks that nothing is more characteristic of the site now than the mounds of brickwork slowly yielding their records. Calvin ties it to the corner and foundation stones: the ruins would serve no new building.

The roaring divides them. Gill reports the view that the Medes and Persians are meant, shouting as they took the city, but objects that the capture was silent; he prefers the Chaldeans, either revelling at the feast during which the city fell, or in the rage with which they offered battle. Ellicott is emphatic that the words do not continue the picture of ruin but carry us to the revelry before the capture, the princes roaring over their prey like young lions. Calvin makes the lions an anticipated objection: they had been superior to all nations, so how could a power so invincible perish? Though lions, their roaring would avail nothing.

The feast in their heat draws out the historians. Gill gives three constructions from Jewish commentators: that the feasts fall in the hot season so the revellers may be made drunk; that when they are hot with feasting the banquet is broken by the writing on the wall; or that their potions are mingled with the wine of wrath. Two ancient historians agree on the feast. Clarke fixes the occasion as a feast in honour of the deity named a few verses later, and notes that since the city fell at night many were slain in their beds. Ellicott calls the words stern and bitter in their irony: when the revellers are hot with wine God calls them to a banquet of another kind, and the cup he gives is the cup of wrath. Wesley adds the vessels taken from the temple. Calvin turns it into evidence: the prophet showed the judgment as by a finger, since no mortal, though endowed a hundred times with the spirit of divination, could have expressed so clearly a thing unknown.

The lambs reverse the lions, and Calvin marks the reversal. In their cry they were lions; in the ease of their destruction, lambs led to the slaughter. He is careful what the figure does not mean: not that they would go gently to a voluntary death, but that however they had threatened others, they would then be women in courage. Ellicott reads the changed figure the same way, the revellers becoming victims of the slaughter-house, the animals standing for the classes of the population, all given to the sword. Gill makes the plainest connection: the drunkenness and perpetual sleep amount to destruction and death. Keil and Delitzsch stand back and name the effect: the fearful destruction of this city will astonish the world.
41:
The cipher name returns and is handled briskly. Ellicott recalls that it stands for Babylon by the letter-code explained earlier in the book, and observes that in the parallelism it balances the actual name in the second clause; the word rendered surprised, he adds, is the one rendered stopped a few verses back. Gill rejects the identification with another city proposed by a scholar he names, since a following clause makes the reference plain, and cites the Targum for support. Clarke offers a different guess, that the city is called by the name of its idol, and glosses the praise of the whole earth by listing the wonders, the height and breadth and compass of the walls, the hanging gardens and the great temple. Wesley says only that it is a name for the city. Keil and Delitzsch supply the frame the exclamation needs, that the verse is an outburst of astonishment at the conquest of a city praised throughout the world, the noun for praise standing for a subject of praise and fame. Calvin makes the exclamation itself a device: the godly, hearing such predictions, would keep asking how this could be, so the prophet anticipates the thought by taking on the character of one filled with wonder, as if to say that though the whole world be astonished, what he predicts is certain.

The sea coming up produces the tile's one flat rejection. Ellicott dismisses the literal reading, which some commentators take of the river flooding, as clearly inadmissible and at variance with the next verse; the prophet falls back on an image he had used before and which an earlier prophet had made familiar, the city covered by a great sea of nations sweeping over her. Gill, Clarke and Wesley all read it the same way, a vast army comparable to the sea for multitude. Keil and Delitzsch note that even the Chaldee paraphrasts took it figuratively, and that one modern scholar alone was inclined to the proper meaning and referred it to the seasonal flooding of the river; but the words speak of no momentary inundation, and the very reason the city is covered with water is that the cities of Babylonia are to become an arid steppe. Calvin explains why the comparison was needed: since it was incredible that the place could be subdued by the forces of men, the calamity is likened to a deluge, the invaders coming with such force that the city is overwhelmed by a flood rather than by an army. Ellicott then finds the paradox the next verse turns on and says the prophet dwells on it with a stern delight: the sea that overflows her shall leave her cities and plains drier and sandier than before, the word for wilderness being the one commonly used of the sandy desert south of the Dead Sea.

On whose cities are meant Gill reports a division. Some understand the one city itself, split into two parts by the river running through it and called by an ancient writer the inward and outward cities; he prefers the rest of the cities of Chaldea, of which this was the mother, the daughters sharing her fate and their ground becoming barren and uncultivated. Calvin reaches the same conclusion, that the threatenings have so far been aimed at the city but the vengeance now extends to every city under that nation's power, and he pauses again to justify his own length: the whole could have been said in a few words, but it was difficult to convince men of what was taught.
44:
The punishment of the god is where the archaeology tells. Gill identifies him as the idol of the Babylonians with a temple in the city, names the classical authors who mention him under a Latinised form, records that some took him for another deity, and dates the punishment to the demolition of the temple, when the golden image was broken up and the gold carried away. Clarke calls him their supreme deity and identifies what he must disgorge, the sacred vessels taken from Jerusalem and dedicated in his temple; on the wall he says only that it shall cease to be a defence and moulder away until in time it is not discernible. Keil and Delitzsch widen the prey to be torn out of the god's jaws beyond the sacred vessels and the voluntary offerings, to all the property Babylon had taken as spoil, and the nations themselves with life and property; his fame, which drew the nations, is destroyed with him. Ellicott makes the same point about the vessels and then supplies the reason the wall is named here rather than merely repeated from an earlier chapter: the two great walls of the city bore names meaning that this god protects and that this is his dwelling, so they were specially consecrated to him as tutelary deity, and he cites the inscriptions for it. Wesley keeps to the vessels and whatever gifts the Babylonians had presented. Calvin will not let the language pass without a caution. God is not properly incensed against idols, which are nothing but things made by men, and a contest with a dead figure void of reason and feeling would be ridiculous; he speaks of it as an enemy for the sake of men, and from that we learn how detestable the false religion was.

The call to come out is dated by Gill with unusual precision. It is not a summons before the capture but after it, when the conqueror issued his proclamation giving liberty to return; many, being well settled, would not be ready to accept, and so are urged to depart because of the danger, since although the city was not destroyed at its taking it was destroyed by a later king. He adds the application to the mystical city. Ellicott notes the emphasis of iteration, the summons having been given twice already, and explains that the fierce anger aimed primarily at Babylon would also fall on those who chose to stay and become partakers of her plagues. Calvin says the exhortation had another purpose besides its plain one, to encourage them in the hope of deliverance, since a free exit was hardly credible and the place was to them like a sepulchre; the faithful were roused this way lest, inebriated with Chaldean indulgences, they should obstinately remain when God stretched out his hand.
46:
The warning against fainting at rumours is read as pastoral. Ellicott corrects the rendering to an imperative, let not your heart faint, and observes that the catastrophe would be preceded by uncertainty; he supplies the news the exiles heard, a king murdered by his successor, that successor killed in battle, a child-king dethroned after months. Clarke dates the rumour to the year before the capture, when the reigning king was defeated in the field. Gill explains the fear, that the Jews had peace in the city's peace and might expect to suffer in its calamities, and answers it: they are to go out and accept the liberty the conqueror grants. Calvin gives the reason the warning was needed: as their minds were raised to the hope of return, great commotions began, the siege bringing something new every day.

The judgment on the images turns on the connecting word. Ellicott insists it has its full force: the exiles were to infer from the rumours just named that the day of vengeance was at hand, the formula announcing days to come being this prophet's customary way of introducing a prediction. He records that some read wounded for slain, the following words indicating they have no power to escape. Gill reports others who connect it with the reports of deliverance that came to nothing while the captives were used more cruelly, and allows the particle may be rendered moreover or surely. Keil and Delitzsch give the logic: the events of the previous verse are harbingers of the judgment. Calvin notes that the sentence widens from the one god named earlier to all of them, and repeats why God raises his hand against inventions of no account: for the sake of men, lest the faithful credit idols when the ungodly are spared.

On the singing of heaven and earth they agree and then argue how literally to take it. Clarke calls the fall a subject of universal rejoicing; Ellicott has the prophet following an earlier one in thinking of the whole creation as rejoicing at the judgment and the people's liberation; Wesley says all the creatures shall rejoice. Calvin calls it a personification, since knowledge is ascribed to heaven and earth, and rejects as frigid the refined explanation that angels and men are meant; the phrase that follows includes the stars, trees, fishes, birds, fields, stones and rivers.

The law of retribution in the next verse is grammatically obscure, and all who touch it say so. Ellicott observes that the interpolated words and the margin both show the construction is difficult, and suggests reading the slain of all the land as giving the law of retribution more emphatically. Calvin canvasses two renderings that turn on dropping a preposition and prefers the simpler: this is the reward rendered to Babylon, that they should fall throughout her land as she had slain Israel. Wesley reaches the same restriction from history, the Chaldeans coming from all parts to help the city being slain there as Israelites had been at Jerusalem.

The final summons is urgent, and the urgency is what they mark. Keil and Delitzsch call the passage the final summing up of the offence and the punishment. Gill identifies the addressees as those who escaped both swords and tells them not to linger. Clarke has them pray for the restoration and embrace the first opportunity of returning. Ellicott reads the command to remember as a demand that in that distant land they still think of Jerusalem as home, and points to a psalm as the exiles' answer by anticipation. Calvin allows that the slaughter would include many of God's people who deserved such an end, and turns the address to those preserved by special favour, assuring them of a return they thought impossible. Wesley says it in a line: leave as soon as liberty is proclaimed, and remember in Judea what God has done.
51:
The confession of shame is put in someone's mouth, and they do not agree whose. Ellicott makes it the answer the prophet hears from the exiles, cast down by the disgrace fallen on them and on the holy city, aliens in blood and faith having profaned the sanctuaries; he had known that bitterness himself and had learnt how to deal with it, answering yes in the verse that follows. Gill hears something less admirable, the Jews objecting to their return or lamenting the desolation, unable to face a land lying waste and an enemy suggesting that their God could not protect them. Wesley makes the shame turn on the reproach cast at their God, and is exact about the trespass: strangers came not to worship but to plunder, into the courts of the priests and into the most holy place. Clarke calls it the lamentation of the pious for the profanation of the temple. Calvin reports the view that the words are a formula given the people to prepare them for return; he prefers anticipation, the prophet repeating what the exiles already said.

What follows is read by all as the answer. Gill says the judgment on the images is designed for their comfort, the gods that reproached the God of Israel being destroyed for that reason. Calvin puts the stake plainly: the design is to raise the minds of the godly so they do not succumb, and God here claims a power that seemed almost to have disappeared, since with the temple overthrown the Babylonians seemed to have triumphed over him. Wesley extends the revenge beyond the idols to their worshippers, with wounded men groaning over all the country. Keil and Delitzsch state the conclusion flatly: Babylon shall by no means escape.

The mounting up to heaven draws out the measurements. Gill has them from an ancient historian: walls two hundred cubits high, towers ten feet higher. Ellicott hears an echo of the builders of the tower that first made the city's name conspicuous, and says that even realised the boast would prove a vain defence; the Greek writers, describing perhaps two lines of fortification, give heights from seventy-five to three hundred and thirty-five feet. Clarke says only that though fortified to the skies it shall fall by the enemies God sends. Calvin turns it into a rule: it is not right to measure God's power by our thoughts, and nothing hinders us more from embracing his promises than considering what may be done naturally, since consulting our own thoughts excludes a power superior to all means.

The cry from the city is heard as already come. Keil and Delitzsch say the prophet sees the destroyers in the spirit as present, a cry of anguish proceeding from the city with great destruction. Gill makes certainty the point, the cry as sure as if already heard. Calvin says the prophet in a manner exults, bringing the faithful to the scene so that they might be assured; he would render the second noun crashing, since a falling mass makes no small noise.

The great voice is glossed four ways. Clarke takes it for the city's pride and boasting; Wesley for the noise of multitudes trafficking together; Ellicott for the stir and tumult of life surging through the streets, identifying the waves as those of the sea of legions, roaring while the voices heard before are hushed in death. Keil and Delitzsch read it the same way, properly the loud voice, the bustle of the city, the waves being the surging masses of the conquering army. Gill ascribes the spoiling to God, who commissioned the Persians as his instruments. Calvin makes the same ascription the point: this is no work of men but God putting forth a power human minds cannot comprehend, the divine name set against all creatures, since what exceeds every human effort is easily done by him.
56:
The new divine title is what Ellicott stops on. The prophet clothes the law of retribution asserted throughout the chapter with a fresh majesty by attaching a new name to it, and God delights, as it were, to manifest himself so: he is a God of recompences and will be true to the title. Clarke says the same in a sentence, that the fall is an act of divine justice and whatever the city suffers it suffers for its crimes. Gill names the spoiler as the Persian with his army; Calvin notices that the noun just used of God is now transferred to the Medes and Persians, the same word serving both because the one ministers for the other. Wesley remarks that little is said here beyond what has been said, except that the wording hints at the surprise.

The drunken princes return to an earlier figure. Ellicott says the imagery is repeated from a few verses back and carries forward a thought from an earlier chapter, and Clarke simply refers back. Gill takes the drunkenness as the wine of divine wrath, that is, their slaughter, while allowing an allusion to the wine at the feast the king made for his thousand lords. Wesley calls it a plain allusion to the posture of the king and his lords while they drank from the vessels brought from the temple. Calvin adds what the historians and another book together supply, that the city was taken that night not only by the besieger's contrivance but through the treachery of men who had revolted from their king.

On the walls the measurements are given again and the source is named. Clarke quotes the historian who saw them: the city a regular square, each side a hundred and twenty stadia, a wall fifty cubits broad and two hundred high, with twenty-five brazen gates to a side; and without the stratagem, he observes, the besieger could not humanly have taken it. Ellicott turns to the gates, part of the works the king prided himself on as restorer of the city, and quotes his inscription: the city is the refuge of the god, the great enclosure is finished, and in the threshold of the great gates folding-doors of brass have been fitted. The clause about labouring in vain, he adds, is all but verbally identical, and in some manuscripts absolutely so, with a verse in one of the minor prophets. Gill explains the preface: because what follows might seem incredible it is introduced by the God of truth. Calvin makes the same point about the eulogy attached to the name: such expressions are designed so that men may rise above everything seen in the world, and not try to contain God's power in their own small measure.
59:
The epilogue is treated as a deliberate sealing of the whole. Calvin calls it exactly that: the prophet not only published what the Spirit dictated but put it in a book, and then delivered the book to a man going to Babylon on the king's business, to read it there and cast it into the river. He draws out what the errand cost: the prophet dared to command the king's messenger, who though meek enough to submit might have been timid and referred the matter to the king, so the act was not without danger and shows invincible courage. Henry marks the same from the other end, that a copy was taken, seemingly by the prophet himself since his usual scribe is not mentioned, and observes how great an advantage it is to the propagating and perpetuating of the word of God that it be written and copied.

The messenger himself is identified with some care. Ellicott says the great prophecy has closed and what remains is an historical appendix; the naming of both father and grandfather leaves no doubt the man was the brother of the prophet's own secretary, which made him the natural depository. The title the received version gives him, taken from a reformer's rendering, really means prince of the resting-place and describes an office like a quartermaster-general. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion and record that the Syriac made him chief of the camp. Gill notes that he is met with nowhere else. Clarke connects the errand to the message sent to the captives. Wesley draws out the chronology: the fourth year was seven years before Jerusalem was taken, so the prophecy stood above sixty years before its first fulfilment. On the book itself Clarke doubts it contained more than the last few verses, and observes that the Hebrew word means any writing great or small; Ellicott insists it was a parchment roll, stress being laid on the whole prophecy standing on one roll, the fitter symbol of the single city. Gill adds that the prophet wrote it himself, his amanuensis not being with him.

Henry works the man's title hardest and reads a character out of it. A prince of rest was one who, holding honour and power, was not like most of the princes then, hot and heady, making parties and heading factions and driving things furiously; he was of a calm temper, studied the things that make for peace, laboured to keep a good understanding between his master and the king of Babylon, and was no persecutor of the prophets but a moderate man. The king was happy in the choice of such an envoy, and the prophet could safely entrust him with an errand of his own; it is the real honour of great men to be quiet men, and the wisdom of princes to put such into places of trust. Henry also supplies the motive for the reading: when the messenger came and saw how large and strong and rich the city was, and was tempted to think it would stand for ever, he was to read the words to himself and his particular friends, that they might see to the end of these threatening powers and comfort one another. Calvin fixes the errand differently and rejects a rabbinic embellishment. The messenger was sent to pacify a king offended by his master's fickleness, an ambassador seeking pardon; the Jewish story that the king himself went is wholly groundless, taken from a book full of fables, and the particle they rest it on will as easily bear from as with, as the versions divide. He dates it seven years before the city was besieged in the ninth year and taken in the eleventh.
61:
Who was to hear the reading is settled almost unanimously. Ellicott corrects the rendering first, the Hebrew being better given as see to it and read, since the English leaves it doubtful what is to be seen; the verb implies reading aloud, and the messenger was to read to those whom it concerned, probably a chosen few of his countrymen. That it was read to the Babylonians he calls improbable in the highest degree. Wesley says the same in six words. Calvin argues it out. The reading was not for hearers who would have been doubly deaf, and Hebrew was not likely familiar to the Chaldeans, the languages having great affinity but some difference; since the messenger is bidden to fix his thoughts on God, the reading must have been in a chamber, and he did not undertake the office of a preacher. He proposes a punctuation too, that one verse and the opening clause of the next stand in a parenthesis, so that the word commanded is the sentence beginning when thou comest to Babylon; and he notes why seeing is mentioned, since the city's splendour might have astonished the messenger.

The words the messenger speaks are read as prayer. Gill takes them for an acknowledgement that the prophecy is of God and a praying over it such as a good man would offer. Ellicott is more exact: they recite predictions from the previous chapter and are an implied prayer, reminding God of what he promised, so that thou hast said becomes the ground of the asking.

The stone bound to the roll is where the tile turns to symbol. Ellicott sets it beside the other acted signs in this book, the girdle, the potter's vessel and the yokes, and explains the mechanics: the roll by itself might have floated and been picked up and read, so the stone was tied that it might sink at once; he traces the symbol into the apocalypse. Calvin reads it as confirmation of faith, and not for the messenger alone. The people were to know that the king's envoy was also the messenger of God and of the prophet, who might otherwise have been despised; and though long unknown, the messenger afterwards acknowledged it. Gill has him not only use the sign but explain it to the friends who accompanied him, and in the name of the Lord. Clarke calls it the emblem of an irretrievable ruin and supplies a pagan parallel: a people resolving to leave their country for ever threw a mass of iron into the sea and swore not to return until it should rise and float.

The last words are the compiler's, and everyone notices. Ellicott observes that the closing clause repeats verbatim the words that ended the prophecy a few verses earlier, and concludes that the messenger was to say those last words and fling the roll into the river as they passed his lips, the submersion typifying the end of the doomed city's futile labour. Of the final sentence he is blunt: it is what we should call an editorial note by whoever compiled the prophecies, careful to tell his readers that the narrative following was not written by the prophet. Wesley defines the term: the words meant are the prophetical ones, since the next chapter is historical and the book of lamentations is not prophecy. Calvin builds a general account of the book on it. The prophets, after speaking in the temple, collected brief summaries containing the principal things, and from these the prophetic books were made up; the volume was not written as we now have it, and does not stand in the order the words were spoken. The scribes collected the summaries affixed to the temple doors and added this conclusion, which in his view is not to be confined to the prophecies about the fall of the city.
